newsitem.title: USA: Lead runs against well-funded rival in EV car race.
newsitem.headline: Lead runs against well-funded rival in EV car race.

text.p: Next month the lead industry will raise a cheer as General Motors launches the first purpose built electric vehicle, but down the road other battery metals are revving up in a bid to overtake the heavy metal.

"This is a very significant factor - it's the first of the major motor manufacturers to design an electric vehicle from the ground up," said Patrick Moseley, program manager for the Advanced Lead Acid Battery Consortium.
The consortium is an alliance of lead producers, battery makers, component manufacturers and utilities.

A traditional gasoline-driven car has a lead-acid battery containing 9 kilograms of lead. The EV's battery will use 270 kilos of the metal - a healthy increase in lead usage but unlikely to prompt a big hike in demand anytime soon.
General Motors has not said how big its EV production run will be. Market demand will determine production, it has said.
GM's EV will be launched at selected sites in California and Arizona, Moseley said. "The production run is real - it will be hundreds, not just ones or twos."
Moseley, who has driven the new car, said it can accelerate from zero to sixty miles and hour in eight seconds, The lead battery lasts for 70 to 75 miles in traffic driving.
Battery life is about two years but because all of General Motors EVs will be leased and not sold, the battery replacement cost is included in the leasing charge, Moseley said.
The battery takes a few minutes for a 50-percent recharge, but three and a half hours to charge fully.

Nevertheless, last month U.S. energy secretary Hazel O'Leary signed a $106 million four-year agreement with the Big Three automakers to back research by the U.S. Advanced Battery Consortium into a battery for electric cars to compete with gasoline vehicles.
The rival consortium, an alliance between the Big Three and the Electric Power Research Institute, is developing nickel metal hydride and lithium ion and polymer batteries for electric vehicles.
Officials from the consortium were not available for comment.

But one nickel battery source said the key aim was make nickel metal hydride batteries cheaper. At present they cost about two to three times more than lead batteries, but much of the arithmetic depends on the size of the production run.

Meanwhile, the Advanced Lead Acid Battery Consortium is starting a new three-year research program in January to double the life of EV lead batteries to four years. Research funds total $17.5 million, a fraction of what the rival consortium is spending but the lead battery is already more advanced than its nickel or lithium counterparts.
Both consortiums see fast-charging and long-battery life as key objective for any consumer friendly product.
Moseley said lead batteries will always have a significant share of the electric vehicle market, no matter what the rival research consortium comes up with.
"Lead batteries are at the most advanced stage of development, they are the cheapest, and they have the highest power."
